title: Nine Fake Names. A Burned Body. She Still Has No Name.
style: vintage collage motion (paper, cut-out archive photos, typewriter, red marker, redaction bars, 12 fps jitter, parallax)
lines: She had nine fake names. Every label scraped off her clothes. And when they found her, half burned in a frozen valley, nobody could say who she was.
November 29th, 1970. Bergen, Norway. A professor and his two young daughters are hiking in a valley the locals call Death Valley.
Among the rocks, they find a woman's body. The front of her body is badly burned. Around her, a melted umbrella, a fur hat, an empty bottle of liquor.
But someone had removed the labels from everything. Her clothes. The bottles. Everything.
The autopsy found dozens of sleeping pills in her body, and smoke in her lungs. There was a bruise on her neck.
Three days later, police found her two suitcases at Bergen's train station.
Inside were wigs. Glasses with plain glass lenses. Five hundred German marks hidden in the lining. And a notebook, written in code.
The code was cracked quickly. It was a list of dates and places. She had been moving across Norway, and across Europe.
Hotels confirmed it. She had checked in under at least nine different names, with nine fake passports.
Staff remembered her as elegant and quiet, about thirty, speaking German, French, Flemish and English. She kept asking to change rooms.
On November 23rd, she checked out of a Bergen hotel, paid in cash, and walked away. Six days later, she was dead in the valley.
Police ruled it a suicide. But how do you set yourself on fire after swallowing that many pills? And why erase your whole identity first?
Then came the spy theory. This was the Cold War. And some of the places she visited matched secret Norwegian missile tests.
Nobody could prove it. In February 1971, she was buried in a Catholic ceremony. Only police officers came.
They buried her in a zinc coffin, so that one day she could be studied again. In 2016, the case was reopened.
Scientists studied her teeth. The chemistry inside them showed she was born around 1930, near Nuremberg, Germany, and grew up toward the French border.
Investigators shared her DNA with the world, hoping for a match.
And yet, more than fifty years later, no one has been able to give her a name.

Who do you think she was? A spy, a smuggler, or someone running from her past? Tell me in the comments. Then watch our Somerton Man short, the man on the beach with no name. And follow for a new mystery every day.

notes: Sources: Wikipedia 'Isdal Woman'; BBC/NRK 'Death in Ice Valley' (2018); NRK 2016-2017 reporting; Mental Floss; All That's Interesting (updated Sep 2025: still unidentified). Body found 29 Nov 1970 in Isdalen ('Death Valley') near Bergen by a professor and his two daughters; front badly burned; items nearby incl. empty St. Hallvard liqueur bottle, plastic bottles, umbrella, fur hat; labels removed from clothes and items. Autopsy: ~50-70 Fenemal (phenobarbital) pills + carbon monoxide; bruise on neck. Two suitcases found at Bergen railway station left-luggage (2 Dec): wigs, non-prescription glasses (her fingerprint), 500 Deutsche Mark in the lining, coded notebook (decoded as dates/places of her travels). At least 9 aliases / fake passports; hotel staff: well dressed, ~30-40, spoke German, French, Flemish, English; changed rooms. Checked out of Hotel Rosenkrantz, Bergen, 23 Nov 1970, paid cash. Police ruled suicide. Spy theory: some travel matched Norwegian Penguin missile tests. Buried 5 Feb 1971, Møllendal cemetery, Catholic rites, zinc coffin; police officers attended. Reopened 2016; 2017 isotope analysis of teeth: born ~1930 (±4) near Nuremberg, moved toward the French/German border region as a child. Still unidentified (no identification reported as of 2025/2026).
